Exercise 5: Clean up

  1. Check local images docker images

    What about images that are not tagged or only exist as intermediate layers?

    Show all imagesdocker images -a

    How much space are your images taking up in total?

    Show the total size of your imagesdocker system df gives you an overview of how much disk space Docker is using, including the total size of all your images. docker images also shows the size of each individual image.
  2. Remove images Try removing one of your images by name:

    docker rmi iris-train:latest

    Question: The image is still listed by docker images. Why?
    AnswerRemoving an image by name only removes that tag. If the same image has other tags (like latest and the registry name jeppetk/iris-train:initial), the image itself is still referenced by the remaining tags and stays on disk.

    Now try removing it by image id instead:

    docker rmi 90c46295c455

    What happens?Removing by image id deletes the image completely (all tags pointing to it are removed), as long as nothing else references it.

    Did you get an error like image is being used by stopped container?

    The common issue: images attached to containersYou cannot remove an image that a container is based on. This goes for running containers too: if you try docker rmi on an image that a running container uses, Docker refuses with image is being used by running container — and even docker rmi -f cannot fully delete it while the container is running. You need to stop the container first, remove it (see step 3), and then remove the image. docker rmi -f does force removal past stopped containers — use with care.
  3. Remove containers Stopped containers pile up quickly. Remove one by name or id:

    docker rm <CONTAINER_ID>

    Or all stopped containers at once:

    docker container prune

    Question: What happens to the data the container wrote to a mounted volume?
    AnswerNothing! Removing a container does not delete your data. Anything written to a volume or bind mount (like -v ./artifacts:/usr/local/app/artifacts) still lives on your computer, and you can access it again from a new container mounting the same volume.

    The -v flag on docker rm exists for the opposite reason: docker rm -v <CONTAINER_ID> removes the anonymous volumes that Docker created for the container. Named volumes and bind mounts are never touched, so your mounted data stays on your computer either way.

  4. Prune images and containers Docker offers a broom for sweeping everything unused away in one go:

    docker image prune

    docker container prune

    You may have seen the word dangling in the output. What does it mean?

    What dangling images areA dangling image is an image layer that no longer has a tag and is not referenced by any tagged image. This typically happens when you rebuild an image with the same tag (like latest): the old image loses its tag and becomes <none>:<none>. They show up in docker images as <none> and are safe candidates for cleanup.

    Warning: pruning cannot be undone. Usually that is fine — you can build your own images again from the Dockerfile, and pull the rest down again. But an image with no Dockerfile behind it is gone for good. docker image prune -a removes all unused images, not just dangling ones, so think twice before adding -a.
